stages.title: Macroeconomic objectives and policies
stages.sub: After this, the student can identify fiscal and monetary policy tools and two further government objectives.

steps.q: A government spends £500bn this year but only collects £450bn in tax. What is the gap between the two called?

steps.q: A government wants spending to equal tax revenue each year, neither running a deficit nor piling up a surplus. What is it aiming for?
steps.right: A balance between what it spends and what it raises
steps.wrong: Spending as little as possible every year
steps.hint: It is not about cutting spending to zero, it is about the two figures matching.

steps.q: The central bank keeps cutting interest rates until they are almost zero, and spending still has not picked up. Is there much room left to cut rates any further?
steps.right: No, there is barely any room left
steps.wrong: Yes, there is plenty of room left
steps.hint: Rates cannot easily go far below zero, so how much lower can they push from here?

steps.q: With rates stuck near zero, the central bank instead creates new money electronically and uses it to buy government bonds from banks, hoping banks then lend more out. What happens to the total amount of money in the economy?
steps.hint: The central bank is creating money, not just moving existing money between accounts.

steps.q: So when a central bank creates new money to buy bonds because cutting rates further is no longer possible, what should we call this extra monetary tool?
steps.right: A separate instrument from cutting rates
steps.wrong: Just another way of cutting rates
steps.hint: It works through buying assets to create money, not through moving the interest rate itself.

steps.q: In a country, the richest 10% earn 40 times more than the poorest 10%. If the government wants to narrow that gap between rich and poor, what is it trying to achieve?
steps.right: Greater equality of income across the population
steps.wrong: Faster growth in total national income
steps.hint: The goal here is about the gap between rich and poor, not the total size of income.
